title: What is the Problem with Marking Criteria?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that abstract marking criteria are the common cause of marker disagreement, odd grades and confused peer assessment, citing Ofqual evidence that senior examiners agree on English grades only half the time. His proposed fix, pending comparative judgement, is concrete success criteria in the form of simple plans of attack. He offers an extract from his book The Full English showing a chronological plan for the literature extract question and a six-step zoom method for description writing, with a worked model answer. He is candid that he has since abandoned the zoom method as type 2 teaching, preferring the simpler video-camera idea, and that a plan must fit what real expertise in English looks like regardless of the exam.
points: Abstract marking criteria produce unreliable marking; concrete, unambiguous success criteria are a more teachable alternative.
A good plan of attack is as simple as possible and consistent with expert views of success in the subject, not just the exam.
Starting an essay with the extract would wreck a chronological argument, so the plan changes the quality of thinking, not just the structure.
Salles flags his own earlier methods as type 2 teaching and simplifies further, modelling a willingness to revise.
quotes: There is a common cause. Marking criteria are abstract. Totally open to interpretation. So open to interpretation that Ofqual’s research shows English is the worst marked GCSE nationally. Senior examiners only award the same grade as other examiners 50% of the time.

But for now, I want to propose another solution. Success criteria which are not abstract, but concrete. Success criteria which are clear and simple things to do - no ambiguity, no need for interpretation.
Sadly, we are stuck with an exam system. A plan of attack is the name I give to a strategy which works for that question, every single time.

Now we can see that “starting with the extract” would completely ruin this chronological argument. Conversely, planning it chronologically has led to a multi-layered analysis of Dickens’ purpose. You can also see how starting with the extract would also encourage students only to focus on the fear produced by the ghosts – in my view a very limited understanding of the text and Dickens’ perspective.

Your job is to find a plan of attack for each question. There are two caveats here: · The plan has to be as simple as possible. · The plan should fit with your expert view of what it is to be successful at English regardless of the exam system in place at the time.

I have now abandoned this sort of method, (as type 2 teaching) because I’ve looked at how real writers write longer descriptions in books. They simply approach the description as a journey through a scene.

Although I am very happy with this technique, some students have found it needlessly complex. There is too much to the plan of attack, whereas simply asking them to place a video camera in six different places in the scene would be much simpler for students to follow. It is almost impossible to misconstrue.
